sanskrit: ॐ केनेषितं पतति प्रेषितं मनः केन प्राणः प्रथमः प्रैति युक्तः । केनेषितां वाचमिमां वदन्ति चक्षुः श्रोत्रं क उ देवो युनक्ति ॥
title: The Source of Mind and Senses
english: By whose impulse does the directed mind go forth? At whose bidding does the foremost vital breath proceed? By whom is this speech prompted? What shining power directs eye and ear?
focus: The inquiry concerns what enables the faculties to function, rather than another object perceived by those faculties.
anchor: Notice both a sensation and the fact that you are aware of it.
iast: oṃ keneṣitaṃ patati preṣitaṃ manaḥ kena prāṇaḥ prathamaḥ praiti yuktaḥ | keneṣitāṃ vācamimāṃ vadanti cakṣuḥ śrotraṃ ka u devo yunakti ||
sourceNote: Om is included as in Shlokam; Wisdomlib writes the same syllable ओं. Vedic pitch accents are not reproduced in this reader.

words.meaning: goes towards; literally, falls or alights.
directs; engages; joins to an activity.

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: The questioner seeks an unchanging principle beyond the changing body, mind and senses. Śaṅkara reads both “impelled” and “directed” as significant: the inquiry is whether the faculties act independently or depend on something beyond their combination. Their activity alone does not establish their independence; the mind can pursue harmful objects even when a person wishes otherwise. Prāṇa is called foremost because the senses depend on its activity.

commentaries.author: Swami Sarvananda
commentaries.text: The inquiry asks whether there is a principle even behind the mind that gives the mind and senses their power to function. The object of inquiry is therefore not simply another mental act.

sanskrit: श्रोत्रस्य श्रोत्रं मनसो मनो यद् वाचो ह वाचं स उ प्राणस्य प्राणः । चक्षुषश्चक्षुरतिमुच्य धीराः प्रेत्यास्माल्लोकादमृता भवन्ति ॥
title: The Ear of the Ear
english: It is the ear of the ear, the mind of the mind, the speech of speech, the life of the vital breath, and the eye of the eye. Relinquishing identification with these, the wise depart from this world and become immortal.
focus: The repeated “of the” distinguishes a faculty from the conscious principle through which its activity is known. The verse does not identify the Self with an organ.
anchor: Listen without reducing awareness to the sound or the ear.
iast: śrotrasya śrotraṃ manaso mano yad vāco ha vācaṃ sa u prāṇasya prāṇaḥ | cakṣuṣaścakṣuratimucya dhīrāḥ pretyāsmāllokādamṛtā bhavanti ||
sourceNote: Complete mantra checked against the Sarvananda PDF linked below and the linked Sanskrit witnesses.

words.meaning: which; that which; because (according to the construction).
indeed; traditionally, it is said (a Vedic particle).
having released oneself; having relinquished identification.

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: “Ear of the ear” does not posit another physical organ. The ear’s capacity to hear depends on the illuminating consciousness of the Self; the same applies to thought, speech, breath and sight. Śaṅkara takes “relinquishing” to mean giving up the mistaken identification of the Self with these instruments. Liberation follows knowledge of their conscious ground, not the mere abandonment of the organs.
commentaries.quote: this capability of the ear depends upon the intelligence of the Atman

commentaries.author: Swami Sarvananda
commentaries.text: The note describes the senses as inert instruments animated by consciousness. Their varied activities indicate a conscious principle that cannot itself be characterized by the attributes of an organ. Relinquishing identification with the instruments is essential to the verse’s promise of immortality.

commentaries.author: Swami Chinmayananda
commentaries.location: Kenopanishad Yajna Prasad, vol. 4, p. 130, as reproduced by Chinmaya Archives
commentaries.text: Chinmayananda distinguishes the life-centre enabling sight, hearing and speech from the limited instruments through which it appears. The source of their power is not confined by their limitations. This archived explanation is placed here for its direct connection with “ear of the ear.”

commentaries.author: Swami Vivekananda
commentaries.location: Soul, Nature and God, opening discussion of perception
commentaries.text: Vivekananda observes that sound can reach the ear without being noticed when the mind is occupied elsewhere. He distinguishes the external instrument, the organ, attention and intellect from the conscious Self. This is a parallel explanation of perception, not a claim that he wrote a bhāṣya on this verse.

sanskrit: न तत्र चक्षुर्गच्छति न वाग्गच्छति नो मनः । न विद्मो न विजानीमो यथैतदनुशिष्यात् । अन्यदेव तद्विदितादथो अविदितादधि । इति शुश्रुम पूर्वेषां ये नस्तद्व्याचचक्षिरे ॥
title: Beyond the Known and Unknown
english: The eye does not reach it, nor speech, nor mind. We do not know; we do not understand how one might teach it. It is different from the known and beyond the unknown. Thus we have heard from the earlier teachers who explained it to us.
focus: This edition keeps both parts together, as Sarvananda and Sitarama Sastri do. Brahman is not another item within the categories of known and unknown; the passage also acknowledges instruction received from teachers.
anchor: Consider why the knower cannot be approached in exactly the same way as a known object.
iast: na tatra cakṣurgacchati na vāggacchati no manaḥ | na vidmo na vijānīmo yathaitadanuśiṣyāt | anyadeva tadviditādatho aviditādadhi | iti śuśruma pūrveṣāṃ ye nastadvyācacakṣire ||
sourceNote: Sarvananda and Sitarama Sastri combine both parts as 1.3. Shlokam and Sanskrit Documents number them 1.3 and 1.4. Punctuation permits the pause form मनः and अनुशिष्यात्; continuous editions join them as मनो न and अनुशिष्यादन्यदेव.

words.meaning: this; that which is under discussion.
thus; marks the end of quoted speech or a designation.
of or from the earlier teachers.

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: A faculty cannot make its own Self an external object. Speech ordinarily identifies things through class, quality or activity, but these cannot delimit Brahman. Śaṅkara therefore turns to instruction received from teachers: Brahman is distinct from both the manifest known and the unmanifest unknown. This does not make Brahman absent; it prevents the disciple from seeking the Self as something to acquire or discard.

commentaries.author: Swami Sarvananda
commentaries.text: Ordinary knowledge distinguishes a subject from an object, whereas the Self is the knowing subject. Sarvananda distinguishes such object-knowledge from immediate realization. He gives two readings of “unknown”: the unmanifest causal condition, and unknown objects generally. The Self is not contained in either category.

commentaries.author: Swami Chinmayananda
commentaries.text: This image illustrates the inadequacy of language to express the Infinite, the difficulty raised by this mantra. The archive presents it as a Kena teaching without specifying a verse number.
commentaries.quote: We cannot produce the war of rolling thunders through the frail melodies of a flute!!

sanskrit: यद्वाचाऽनभ्युदितं येन वागभ्युद्यते । तदेव ब्रह्म त्वं विद्धि नेदं यदिदमुपासते ॥
title: That Which Enables Speech
english: What speech does not express, but by which speech is expressed—know that alone as Brahman, not this that people worship as an object.
focus: The refrain distinguishes Brahman, the ground of the worshipper's awareness, from a limited object conceived as separate from that awareness. It is not a dismissal of every form of devotional practice.
anchor: Attend to the awareness present before and during an utterance.
iast: yadvācā’nabhyuditaṃ yena vāgabhyudyate | tadeva brahma tvaṃ viddhi nedaṃ yadidamupāsate ||
sourceNote: Complete mantra checked against the Sarvananda PDF linked below and the linked Sanskrit witnesses.

words.meaning: which; that which; because (according to the construction).
not expressed; not revealed by speech.
is expressed; is brought into activity.
Brahman; the absolute reality (neuter, not the creator Brahmā).
which; that which; because (according to the construction).

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: Śaṅkara addresses the suspicion that Brahman must be a deity apart from the worshipper. Speech expresses limited objects, but Brahman is the consciousness enabling speech itself. The refrain directs the student to the unconditioned Self rather than an object designated as “this.” Descriptions such as “speech of speech” are indications through the faculties, not attributes that confine Brahman.

commentaries.author: Swami Sarvananda
commentaries.text: The following five mantras indicate Brahman indirectly through the faculties. Sarvananda reads “this” as something with name and form, conceived as separate from its worshipper. The intended recognition is of Brahman as one’s own conscious being, beyond such objectification. His note explicitly connects this recognition with transcending the senses and mind.

sanskrit: यन्मनसा न मनुते येनाहुर्मनो मतम् । तदेव ब्रह्म त्वं विद्धि नेदं यदिदमुपासते ॥
title: That Which Enables Thought
english: What one cannot think with the mind, but by which, they say, the mind is known—know that alone as Brahman, not this that people worship as an object.
focus: The mind can be noticed through its changing thoughts. This verse turns inquiry towards that in whose presence those thoughts are known.
anchor: Observe a thought arise and pass; distinguish its content from knowing it.
iast: yanmanasā na manute yenāhurmano matam | tadeva brahma tvaṃ viddhi nedaṃ yadidamupāsate ||
sourceNote: Complete mantra checked against the Sarvananda PDF linked below and the linked Sanskrit witnesses.

words.meaning: which; that which; because (according to the construction).
Brahman; the absolute reality (neuter, not the creator Brahmā).
which; that which; because (according to the construction).

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: Here “mind” includes the inner instrument’s different activities. Its thoughts and determinations become manifest through the consciousness of the Self; the mind does not, in turn, illuminate Brahman as an object. Śaṅkara connects this mantra with the preceding refrain: recognize the inner conscious principle rather than treating a mental conception as Brahman itself.

commentaries.author: Swami Sarvananda
commentaries.text: The note distinguishes the mind’s reception of sensory impressions from the conscious principle by which they become known. It also offers a simpler formulation: the mind derives its power of understanding from the Self. “Mind” here covers the whole inner instrument, not only one of its functions.

sanskrit: यच्चक्षुषा न पश्यति येन चक्षूँषि पश्यति । तदेव ब्रह्म त्वं विद्धि नेदं यदिदमुपासते ॥
title: That Which Enables Sight
english: What one does not see with the eye, but by which the eyes see—know that alone as Brahman, not this that people worship as an object.
focus: Brahman is not a special visible object. The teaching concerns the basis of seeing, and the Sanskrit repeats “sees” on both sides of that distinction.
anchor: Look at something ordinary and attend to the fact of seeing.
iast: yaccakṣuṣā na paśyati yena cakṣūm̐ṣi paśyati | tadeva brahma tvaṃ viddhi nedaṃ yadidamupāsate ||
sourceNote: चक्षूँषि retains the source’s Vedic nasal notation; the separated word is shown as चक्षूंषि.

words.meaning: which; that which; because (according to the construction).
eyes; faculties of sight. The continuous text uses Vedic nasalization: चक्षूँषि.
Brahman; the absolute reality (neuter, not the creator Brahmā).
which; that which; because (according to the construction).

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: To “see” something ordinarily means to perceive it as an object. Śaṅkara distinguishes this from the consciousness by which the eye’s activity is known. That activity varies with the mind, while the Self illuminates it. Thus Brahman is indicated through seeing without becoming something visible alongside other objects.

sanskrit: यच्छ्रोत्रेण न शृणोति येन श्रोत्रमिदं श्रुतम् । तदेव ब्रह्म त्वं विद्धि नेदं यदिदमुपासते ॥
title: That Which Enables Hearing
english: What one does not hear with the ear, but by which this hearing is known—know that alone as Brahman, not this that people worship as an object.
focus: The repetition of the same refrain across the faculties is deliberate. None of the senses makes Brahman into an object, yet each depends on the reality being indicated.
anchor: Listen for a sound, then notice the awareness of its absence.
iast: yacchrotreṇa na śṛṇoti yena śrotramidaṃ śrutam | tadeva brahma tvaṃ viddhi nedaṃ yadidamupāsate ||
sourceNote: The reading श्रोत्रमिदं श्रुतम् agrees with the Sarvananda PDF linked below, Shlokam and Sanskrit Documents; the Wisdomlib web transcription has a typographical corruption here.

words.meaning: which; that which; because (according to the construction).
Brahman; the absolute reality (neuter, not the creator Brahmā).
which; that which; because (according to the construction).

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: Śaṅkara describes hearing as the activity of the ear in conjunction with the mind. Brahman is not a sound presented to this faculty. Rather, the ear and its activity are themselves disclosed through the intelligence of the Self. The explanation of the repeated refrain carries forward from the earlier mantras on speech and thought.

sanskrit: यत्प्राणेन न प्राणिति येन प्राणः प्रणीयते । तदेव ब्रह्म त्वं विद्धि नेदं यदिदमुपासते ॥
title: That Which Directs Breath
english: What one does not breathe with the breath, but by which the breath is directed—know that alone as Brahman, not this that people worship as an object.
focus: Prāṇa can indicate vital breath; in a sensory reading it can refer to the faculty of smell. Sarvananda explicitly notes both interpretations. Neither reading makes Brahman a thing inhaled.
anchor: Notice breathing without trying to turn its conscious ground into another sensation.
iast: yatprāṇena na prāṇiti yena prāṇaḥ praṇīyate | tadeva brahma tvaṃ viddhi nedaṃ yadidamupāsate ||
sourceNote: Complete mantra checked against the Sarvananda PDF linked below and the linked Sanskrit witnesses.

words.meaning: which; that which; because (according to the construction).
by the vital breath; by the faculty of smell in a sensory interpretation.
breathes; in the sensory interpretation, smells.
Brahman; the absolute reality (neuter, not the creator Brahmā).
which; that which; because (according to the construction).

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: Śaṅkara takes prāṇa here in the sensory setting of the breath moving through the nostrils and the perception of odour. Brahman is not something smelled; it is the consciousness through which that faculty is directed towards its objects. This reading completes the sequence of faculties rather than making Brahman another object available to one of them.

commentaries.author: Swami Sarvananda
commentaries.text: Sarvananda explicitly allows prāṇa to mean the sense of smell here, alongside the reading in terms of vital breath. He also observes that these last five mantras directly answer the questions posed in the opening mantra.

sanskrit: यदि मन्यसे सुवेदेति दभ्रमेवापि नूनं त्वं वेत्थ ब्रह्मणो रूपम् । यदस्य त्वं यदस्य देवेष्वथ नु मीमाँस्यमेव ते मन्ये विदितम् ॥
title: The Need for Further Inquiry
english: If you think “I know it well,” you know only a little of Brahman's form—its appearance in yourself and among the gods. It still calls for inquiry. [The pupil, after reflection:] “I think I have understood.”
focus: The teacher questions premature certainty. The final words are read here as the pupil's response, following Sarvananda's explanation; some English renderings attach the sentence differently.
anchor: Distinguish understanding a description from recognizing what it points to.
section: Inquiry and the limits of certainty
iast: yadi manyase suvedeti dabhramevāpi nūnaṃ tvaṃ vettha brahmaṇo rūpam | yadasya tvaṃ yadasya deveṣvatha nu mīmām̐syameva te manye viditam ||
sourceNote: दभ्रमेवापि follows the Sarvananda PDF linked below and is a variant recorded by Shlokam. The Sitarama Sastri web transcription and Shlokam’s primary reading have दहरमेवापि. मीमाँस्यम् is shown as मीमांस्यम् in the separated-word view.

words.meaning: thus; marks the end of quoted speech or a designation.
little; a limited measure. Another reading is दहरम्.
which; that which; because (according to the construction).
which; that which; because (according to the construction).
indeed; a particle emphasizing the inquiry.
to be investigated; deserving further inquiry.

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: The teacher challenges a premature claim of complete knowledge. Brahman cannot become an object for a separate knower, just as fire does not burn itself. What the disciple knows as a human or divine manifestation is limited by its conditions. Śaṅkara describes the pupil withdrawing to reflect on the teaching, test its meaning and return with a more exact understanding.

commentaries.author: Swami Sarvananda
commentaries.text: The warning is directed against mistaking the ego for the Self. Although the ego appears to be the subject of experience, Sarvananda treats it as a modification of the intellect, illuminated by the Self. Alternatively, the warning concerns merely intellectual comprehension. The disciple must carry inquiry beyond that limited grasp.

sanskrit: नाहं मन्ये सुवेदेति नो न वेदेति वेद च । यो नस्तद्वेद तद्वेद नो न वेदेति वेद च ॥
title: Knowing Without Claiming Mastery
english: I do not think “I know it well”; nor is it that I do not know it. I know it too. Whoever among us understands this understands it: not that I do not know it, and yet I know it.
focus: The pupil distinguishes ordinary knowledge of an object from the inseparable awareness of one's own existence. The repeated clauses belong to the text and must not be collapsed into one occurrence.
anchor: Consider the difference between being aware and claiming exhaustive knowledge of awareness.
section: Inquiry and the limits of certainty
iast: nāhaṃ manye suvedeti no na vedeti veda ca | yo nastadveda tadveda no na vedeti veda ca ||
sourceNote: Complete mantra checked against the Sarvananda PDF linked below and the linked Sanskrit witnesses.

words.meaning: thus; marks the end of quoted speech or a designation.
know; in the quoted first-person clauses: I know; with यः or तत्: knows.
thus; marks the end of quoted speech or a designation.
know; in the quoted first-person clauses: I know; with यः or तत्: knows.
know; in the quoted first-person clauses: I know; with यः or तत्: knows.
know; in the quoted first-person clauses: I know; with यः or तत्: knows.
know; in the quoted first-person clauses: I know; with यः or तत्: knows.
thus; marks the end of quoted speech or a designation.
know; in the quoted first-person clauses: I know; with यः or तत्: knows.

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: The disciple’s answer is not a recommendation of doubt or error. Śaṅkara reads it as a firm recognition supported by the teacher’s instruction, reasoning and the disciple’s own realization. Brahman is neither an ordinarily known object nor wholly unknown, since it is the Self. The apparently conflicting clauses preserve this distinction rather than cancelling each other.

commentaries.author: Swami Sarvananda
commentaries.text: Brahman cannot be classified and differentiated as ordinary objects can. Yet its complete absence from knowledge cannot be asserted, since it is one’s own Self and every act of knowing presupposes it. Sarvananda presents these two features together as the point of the disciple’s answer.

sanskrit: यस्यामतं तस्य मतं मतं यस्य न वेद सः । अविज्ञातं विजानतां विज्ञातमविजानताम् ॥
title: Known Through Not-Knowing
english: It is understood by the one for whom it is not grasped as an object; the one who thinks it so grasped does not know it. It is unknown to those who claim to know, and known to those who do not claim that kind of knowledge.
focus: The apparent paradox concerns the manner of knowing. It does not praise lack of inquiry or mere ignorance.
anchor: Notice any attempt to possess the Self as a mental image.
section: From the paradox of knowing to realization
iast: yasyāmataṃ tasya mataṃ mataṃ yasya na veda saḥ | avijñātaṃ vijānatāṃ vijñātamavijānatām ||
sourceNote: Complete mantra checked against the Sarvananda PDF linked below and the linked Sanskrit witnesses.

words.meaning: not grasped as a thought or object.
knows; I know (as spoken in the first-person passages).
of those who suppose they know.
of those who do not claim such objectifying knowledge.

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: The Upaniṣad now confirms the understanding shared by teacher and disciple. To suppose that Brahman is known as a bounded object is to confuse it with the senses, mind or intellect. Śaṅkara distinguishes this mistake from simple ignorance: the problem is specifically the conviction that such a conditioned thing is the Self. Recognizing that limitation is central to the verse’s paradox.

commentaries.author: Swami Sarvananda
commentaries.text: Sarvananda distinguishes realization from confidence in a merely phenomenal self. He specifically reports Śaṅkara’s qualification that the mistaken “knowers” are those who identify the Self with mind, intellect or senses, rather than people who have never considered the question at all.

commentaries.author: S. Radhakrishnan
commentaries.location: The Principal Upaniṣads, Kena 2.3, printed pp. 585–586
commentaries.text: Radhakrishnan reads the paradox as exposing the limits of human expression and mental formulation. His note compares it with other traditions that distinguish direct spiritual realization from claiming to comprehend the divine as an object.

sanskrit: प्रतिबोधविदितं मतममृतत्वं हि विन्दते । आत्मना विन्दते वीर्यं विद्यया विन्दतेऽमृतम् ॥
title: Known in Every Cognition
english: It is rightly known when recognized in every cognition; through this one attains immortality. Through the Self one gains strength; through knowledge one gains immortality.
focus: Pratibodha-viditam means known with reference to each cognition. The three occurrences of vindate carry the progression from immortality, through strength, to immortality again.
anchor: Attend to the awareness common to changing perceptions.
section: From the paradox of knowing to realization
iast: pratibodhaviditaṃ matamamṛtatvaṃ hi vindate | ātmanā vindate vīryaṃ vidyayā vindate’mṛtam ||
sourceNote: Complete mantra checked against the Sarvananda PDF linked below and the linked Sanskrit witnesses.

words.meaning: known in each cognition; prati-bodha-viditam, recognized with reference to every act of knowing.

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: Śaṅkara explains pratibodha-viditam as recognition with reference to every cognition: the Self is the witness through which changing mental states are known. It is consciousness itself, not an inert substance that occasionally acquires knowledge. Immortality is not a new condition produced in the Self. The strength of Self-knowledge overcomes mortality because it does not depend on perishable external means.
commentaries.quote: Brahman is known as the witness of all states of consciousness

commentaries.author: Swami Sarvananda
commentaries.text: The note identifies Brahman as the unaffected conscious witness behind all mental modifications. Sarvananda explicitly places this realization in the superconscious or samādhi state. He explains the strength mentioned next as the vigour of body and mind arising from constant meditation on the transcendental Self. This particular emphasis belongs to his exposition.

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara · translated by Swami Gambhirananda
commentaries.text: This translation likewise presents the Self as the witness of every mental cognition. It distinguishes consciousness itself from a substance inferred to possess a temporary power of knowing.

commentaries.author: S. Radhakrishnan
commentaries.location: The Principal Upaniṣads, Kena 2.4, printed p. 586
commentaries.text: Following Śaṅkara, Radhakrishnan identifies the Self as the witness underlying every cognition. He contrasts this with inferring an inert substance that intermittently acquires knowledge: the witness is the basis of knowing, not another changing item within it.

sanskrit: इह चेदवेदीदथ सत्यमस्ति न चेदिहावेदीन्महती विनष्टिः । भूतेषु भूतेषु विचित्य धीराः प्रेत्यास्माल्लोकादमृता भवन्ति ॥
title: Realization Here, in All Beings
english: If one realizes it here, there is true fulfilment; if one does not realize it here, the loss is great. Discerning it in every being, the wise depart from this world and become immortal.
focus: Both halves form one complete mantra in the consulted editions. The urgency of realization here belongs with the recognition of the Self in all beings.
anchor: Let attention extend from your own experience to the presence of other beings.
section: From the paradox of knowing to realization
iast: iha cedavedīdatha satyamasti na cedihāvedīnmahatī vinaṣṭiḥ | bhūteṣu bhūteṣu vicitya dhīrāḥ pretyāsmāllokādamṛtā bhavanti ||
sourceNote: Complete mantra checked against the Sarvananda PDF linked below and the linked Sanskrit witnesses.

words.meaning: in beings; repeated to mean in every being.
in beings; repeated to mean in every being.

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: “Here” makes realization a concern of this embodied life. Śaṅkara interprets the great loss as continued involvement in the cycle of birth and death through ignorance. The discerning recognize one Self in moving and unmoving beings and turn from the possessive identification expressed as “I” and “mine.” The two halves belong together: urgency in this life and recognition of unity in all beings.

commentaries.author: Swami Sarvananda
commentaries.text: “Truth” is explained as reaching the true goal of life. The great loss is continued passage through birth and death and their painful consequences. Sarvananda keeps this urgency together with recognition of the Self in all beings.

commentaries.author: S. Radhakrishnan
commentaries.location: The Principal Upaniṣads, Kena 2.5, printed p. 587
commentaries.text: His note emphasizes realization here in embodied life and recognition of the same Brahman in every creature. Failing to discover this leaves one absorbed in the processes of mind and body rather than established in one’s true being.

sanskrit: ब्रह्म ह देवेभ्यो विजिग्ये तस्य ह ब्रह्मणो विजये देवा अमहीयन्त । त ऐक्षन्तास्माकमेवायं विजयोऽस्माकमेवायं महिमेति ॥
title: The Gods Claim the Victory

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: Śaṅkara gives several purposes for the story: it counters the inference that an unobjectifiable Brahman is nonexistent, praises knowledge of Brahman, shows how difficult that knowledge is, and exposes false claims of independent agency. The gods attribute victory to their limited forms. In his account, the power and glory actually belong to the Lord present as their inner Self.

commentaries.author: Swami Sarvananda
commentaries.text: In his concluding inward interpretation of the whole narrative, Sarvananda reads the gods as the beneficial faculties and their opponents as desire and its harmful tendencies. The faculties’ victory depends on the Self, but they mistake their capacities for independent powers. This is a shared allegorical reading of the story, not a literal replacement for its characters.

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: Brahman knows the gods’ mistaken claim. Śaṅkara presents the appearance as an act of compassion: their error is to be removed before it brings them the downfall of the Asuras. The wondrous form is assumed for their benefit. Their inability to identify it reveals the difference between possessing a power and understanding its source.

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: The gods choose Agni because of his brilliance and eminence, expecting him to identify the unfamiliar presence. commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: Agni approaches to inquire but is overawed into silence, so the mysterious presence asks the first question. Śaṅkara hears self-satisfaction in Agni’s reply that he is renowned under two names. Naming himself, however, has not answered the gods’ question about the being before him. This is the identity exchange within the commentary on 3.3–3.6.

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: The question now tests the capacity implied by Agni’s celebrated names. He claims the ability to burn everything on earth. Śaṅkara takes “earth” illustratively rather than as an exclusion of things in the air: the boast is comprehensive. The single straw in the next mantra will put that universal claim to a precise test.

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: The contrast is deliberate: the one who claims to consume everything cannot burn a straw placed before him by Brahman. Śaṅkara describes Agni approaching with great confidence and returning ashamed when that confidence fails. His final report admits the limit of his knowledge as well as of his power. The command, failure and return complete the one episode.

commentaries.author: Swami Sarvananda
commentaries.text: Within his concluding allegory, Agni represents speech claiming the ability to explain the universe. Its failure before the Yakṣa marks the inability of speech to comprehend and explain the Self. This note applies the book’s interpretation of the wider narrative to Agni’s completed test.

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: Śaṅkara says that the explanation of the earlier commission to Agni also applies here. The gods now ask Vāyu to discover the same presence. This is a new attempt within a deliberately parallel narrative, not a new independent explanation of Brahman. His commentary groups Vāyu’s commission, identity, claim and test as 3.7–3.10.

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: Śaṅkara explains Vāyu’s names through movement and space: Mātariśvan is associated with moving in the encompassing space. The remainder is read in parallel with Agni’s self-identification. Both naming clauses belong to Vāyu’s reply, but neither identifies the source of the power he is about to claim.

commentaries.text: Śaṅkara glosses the central verb as the ability to take or carry away and refers the remaining explanation to Agni’s parallel boast. commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: The inability to lift the straw answers Vāyu’s claim to carry away everything. Śaṅkara explicitly applies the explanation of Agni’s test to this parallel episode. Vāyu’s return reports that the presence remains unrecognized. The failure concerns the assumption that a faculty’s power is independently its own, not merely the relative size of the task.

commentaries.author: Swami Sarvananda
commentaries.text: In the same inward reading, Vāyu represents prāṇa, with mind possibly included through its dependence on prāṇa. Its claim to control and comprehend meets the same limit as speech. Sarvananda presents this as an allegorical correspondence, not as extra words in the mantra.

english: Then they said to Indra, “Maghavan, find out what this wondrous being is.” “So be it,” he replied. He ran towards it, but it disappeared from him.
focus: Indra does not receive a third grass test. The disappearance leads into a different way of learning in the next passage.

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: Śaṅkara explains the disappearance before Indra as a further removal of pride: even the lord of the gods cannot command a direct encounter on his own terms. Unlike Agni and Vāyu, Indra does not immediately return. His continued inquiry at that place prepares the encounter with Umā in the next mantra. The source discusses 3.11–3.12 together.

commentaries.author: Swami Sarvananda
commentaries.text: Sarvananda’s closing allegory reads Indra as the individual self. The disappearance points to the dissolution of the subject–object contrast during inward inquiry, rather than the successful capture of a separate object. This is his interpretation of the narrative as a whole.

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: Śaṅkara presents Umā as knowledge appearing in a beautiful form to the still-inquiring Indra. He records explanations of Haimavatī through golden adornment and through her relationship to Himavat. Her association with the omniscient Lord makes her an appropriate teacher. Indra therefore asks her to identify what he himself could not recognize.

commentaries.author: Swami Sarvananda
commentaries.text: In that inward interpretation, Umā represents illuminating knowledge: divine grace in devotional language, and the soul’s power of knowledge in Advaita language. Through her, the individual recognizes Brahman as its own essence. Sarvananda offers this as the culmination of the wider allegory.

sanskrit: सा ब्रह्मेति होवाच ब्रह्मणो वा एतद्विजये महीयध्वमिति ततो हैव विदाञ्चकार ब्रह्मेति ॥

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: Śaṅkara emphasizes the source of Indra’s recognition: he learns that it was Brahman from Umā’s instruction, not independently. Her answer also corrects the gods’ original claim. Their glory was gained through Brahman’s victory, so possession of that glory did not establish that they were its autonomous cause.
commentaries.quote: From her words alone Indra learned that it was Brahman.

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: Agni, Vāyu and Indra are praised for coming closest to the presence through encounter and conversation, and for being the first among the gods to learn what it was. Śaṅkara treats their distinction as a consequence of this approach and knowledge. The passage praises proximity to Brahman, not a successful demonstration of the powers they originally claimed.

title: Indra's Particular Nearness
english: Therefore Indra excels the other gods, as it were: he approached it most closely and was the first to know that it was Brahman.
focus: The preceding collective statement is now focused on Indra, who received Umā's instruction. Both reasons for his distinction are included.
anchor: Consider the role of receiving instruction in recognition.

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: Indra’s distinction is now explained more specifically. He first receives the identification from Umā; Agni and Vāyu subsequently learn through him. Śaṅkara connects Indra’s nearness with being the first to receive this knowledge. The verse’s praise therefore concerns instruction and recognition rather than a superior performance in the straw test.

commentaries.author: Swami Sarvananda
commentaries.text: The note treats the story as praise of Brahman’s supremacy: even the great gods depend on that power. It also reports an interpretation in terms of worship of Brahman with attributes. This comment covers the narrative conclusion, including the distinction given to Indra.

sanskrit: तस्यैष आदेशो यदेतद्विद्युतो व्यद्युतदा३ इतीन् न्यमीमिषदा३ इत्यधिदैवतम् ॥

english: This is the indication of it: like a flash of lightning, like the blink of an eye. This is the teaching with reference to the gods.
focus: These are analogies of sudden manifestation, not definitions of Brahman. The prolonged ā, marked by ३, is read comparatively: “like” or “as it were.” Sarvananda also records an alternative reading in terms of Brahman's command in nature.
anchor: Let the brevity of a flash suggest the limit of holding recognition as an object.

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: Ādeśa is instruction through comparison. Śaṅkara reads the prolonged ā as “like”: the brief manifestation before the gods is likened to a flash of lightning and the opening and closing of an eye. These illustrations indicate the sudden showing and withdrawal of the presence; they do not provide a literal physical definition of the incomparable Brahman.

commentaries.author: Swami Sarvananda
commentaries.text: Sarvananda acknowledges the difficulty created by the compact wording. Alongside Śaṅkara’s comparison with a sudden, fleeting appearance, he records another reading: lightning and other natural activity manifest Brahman’s command. The latter is an alternative interpretation, not the same explanation in different words.

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara · translated by Swami Gambhirananda
commentaries.text: Ādeśa is explained as instruction by analogy, and ā as a comparison. Lightning and the eye’s movement illustrate the brief manifestation; they do not make Brahman dependent on borrowed light.

sanskrit: अथाध्यात्मं यदेतद्गच्छतीव च मनोऽनेन चैतदुपस्मरत्यभीक्ष्णँ सङ्कल्पः ॥
title: The Mind's Repeated Remembrance
english: Now the inward indication: the mind seems to go towards it; through the mind one repeatedly recalls it. Such is the thought or resolve directed towards it.
focus: The “as if” matters: the mind does not travel to Brahman as to a separate physical destination. The Sanskrit verb for recollection is singular upasmarati.
anchor: Return gently to the awareness of the present thought.
iast: athādhyātmaṃ yadetadgacchatīva ca mano’nena caitadupasmaratyabhīkṣṇam̐ saṅkalpaḥ ||
sourceNote: यदेतद् follows the Sarvananda PDF linked below and Shlokam; Sanskrit Documents prints यद्देतद्. उपस्मरति is singular; the former app’s plural IAST was incorrect.

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: The text now turns from cosmic illustrations to the inner instrument. Śaṅkara relates the mind’s recollection and resolve to Brahman as presented through the conditioning mind. Their rapid occurrence supplies an inward analogy to the earlier flash and blink. The illustration helps the learner approach the teaching without making the unconditioned Brahman a bounded mental object.

commentaries.author: Swami Sarvananda
commentaries.text: The inward instruction concerns drawing the mind within and fixing it on the Self with determination. Sarvananda renders the passage as the devotee’s desire that Brahman should be remembered continually as very near.

sanskrit: तद्ध तद्वनं नाम तद्वनमित्युपासितव्यं स य एतदेवं वेदाभि हैनꣳ सर्वाणि भूतानि संवाञ्छन्ति ॥
title: Tadvanam: The Adorable
english: It is called Tadvanam, the adorable; as Tadvanam it should be contemplated. All beings are drawn towards the one who knows it in this way.
focus: The name appears twice in the mantra. The instruction concerns contemplation under that name and its stated fruit.
anchor: Consider what is worthy of love beyond usefulness or possession.
iast: taddha tadvanaṃ nāma tadvanamityupāsitavyaṃ sa ya etadevaṃ vedābhi hainaṃ sarvāṇi bhūtāni saṃvāñchanti ||
sourceNote: Complete mantra checked against the Sarvananda PDF linked below and the linked Sanskrit witnesses.

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: Tadvanam names Brahman as worthy of love and contemplation because it is the Self of all beings. Śaṅkara takes the instruction as meditation under this name, and the following statement as the fruit of that contemplation: beings are drawn to the meditator. The two occurrences of Tadvanam establish the name and then prescribe its contemplative use.

sanskrit: उपनिषदं भो ब्रूहीत्युक्ता त उपनिषद्ब्राह्मीं वाव त उपनिषदमब्रूमेति ॥
title: The Teaching Has Been Given
english: “Sir, teach me the Upaniṣad.” “The Upaniṣad has been told to you. We have indeed told you the Upaniṣad concerning Brahman.”
focus: The teacher confirms the completeness of what has been taught. The second sentence, previously absent from the app, is integral to the reply.
anchor: Review the teaching already given before looking for a further secret.
iast: upaniṣadaṃ bho brūhītyuktā ta upaniṣadbrāhmīṃ vāva ta upaniṣadamabrūmeti ||
sourceNote: Complete mantra checked against the Sarvananda PDF linked below and the linked Sanskrit witnesses.

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: Śaṅkara reads the pupil’s renewed request as asking whether anything further must be combined with the teaching to secure liberation. The teacher’s answer confirms that the knowledge already taught is complete. The disciplines mentioned next prepare a person to acquire that knowledge; they are not additional actions that must manufacture its liberating result.

sanskrit: तस्यै तपो दमः कर्मेति प्रतिष्ठा वेदाः सर्वाङ्गानि सत्यमायतनम् ॥
title: The Foundation and Its Home
english: Austerity, self-control and prescribed action are its foundation; the Vedas are all its limbs; truth is its dwelling place.
focus: The disciplines, the Vedas and truth occur in one complete mantra. They describe the preparation and support for the teaching, not three separate revelations.
anchor: Choose one concrete act of truthfulness or restraint to practise today.
iast: tasyai tapo damaḥ karmeti pratiṣṭhā vedāḥ sarvāṅgāni satyamāyatanam ||
sourceNote: The complete mantra includes foundation, Vedas and truth. तस्यै follows the PDF and Shlokam; Wisdomlib’s तसै is a transcription error.

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: Tapas, restraint and prescribed action purify the mind so that the teaching can be understood rather than disbelieved or misconstrued. Śaṅkara calls them supports for acquiring knowledge, alongside the Vedas and their auxiliary disciplines. Truth receives particular emphasis: freedom from deception in thought, speech and action makes the person a fitting dwelling for this knowledge.
commentaries.quote: freedom from deceit and fraud in speech, mind or deed

commentaries.author: Swami Sarvananda
commentaries.text: The disciplines are the feet of the teaching because they lead to purification of mind, a prerequisite for understanding Self-knowledge. Study of the Vedas supports its understanding in its different aspects. Truth is its dwelling because knowledge can abide in a heart purified by truthfulness.

sanskrit: यो वा एतामेवं वेदापहत्य पाप्मानमनन्ते स्वर्गे लोके ज्येये प्रतितिष्ठति प्रतितिष्ठति ॥
title: Firmly Established
english: Whoever knows this teaching thus, having dispelled evil, becomes firmly established in the limitless, highest, heavenly realm—becomes firmly established.
focus: The closing verb is deliberately repeated. Śaṅkara interprets the highest realm as Brahman; Sarvananda explicitly offers Brahma-loka and gradual liberation as another interpretation. These readings should not be presented as unanimous.
anchor: Read the repeated final words slowly, without turning them into a promise of a particular experience.
iast: yo vā etāmevaṃ vedāpahatya pāpmānamanante svarge loke jyeye pratitiṣṭhati pratitiṣṭhati ||
sourceNote: The Sanskrit is shared, but interpretations of the final realm differ: Śaṅkara identifies it with Brahman; Sarvananda discusses Brahma-loka and gradual liberation.

words.meaning: indeed; certainly. In connected Vedic text before a vowel it appears as वा.

commentaries.author: Śaṅkara
commentaries.text: Śaṅkara interprets the evil overcome as ignorance, desire and action that sustain saṃsāra. “Limitless” and “highest” prevent him from reading the final realm as an ordinary heaven with a finite reward. He identifies it with unconditioned, blissful Brahman. Firm establishment means freedom from returning to the cycle of worldly existence.

commentaries.author: Swami Sarvananda
commentaries.text: Sarvananda explicitly records Śaṅkara’s identification of the highest heaven with Brahman, but then proposes Brahma-loka and gradual liberation as another reading. The two explanations should remain distinct; his alternative should not be quoted as Śaṅkara’s conclusion.
